title: Senior's toolkit: finding and fixing slow queries
summary: Query plans in SQLite and PostgreSQL, the statistics that drive them, finding the worst queries in production, and adding indexes without downtime.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: finding and fixing slow queries
steps.body: Performance work is measure, explain, change, measure again. These are the commands a senior runs when the dashboard is slow, in the order they usually need them.

toolkit.cmd: SELECT query, calls, mean_exec_time, total_exec_time FROM pg_stat_statements
toolkit.what: PostgreSQL's record of every query shape and the time it took (the `pg_stat_statements` extension). Sort by total time to find what costs the most overall, not just the slowest single call.
flags: how often it runs (an N+1 shows up as a huge number)
toolkit.example:
SELECT left(query, 80) AS query, calls, round(mean_exec_time) AS mean_ms, round(total_exec_time) AS total_ms
FROM pg_stat_statements
ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC
LIMIT 10;

toolkit.what: PostgreSQL: run the query and show the real plan with actual times, actual row counts and pages read. ANALYZE really executes it, so wrap an UPDATE or DELETE in `BEGIN; ... ROLLBACK;`.
flags: execute and report actual time and rows
shared hit (from memory) vs read (from disk)
a big gap means bad estimates, usually stale statistics
toolkit.example:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42 ORDER BY placed_at DESC LIMIT 20;

toolkit.what: SQLite: show the plan without running the query. Look for `SCAN` on big tables and `USE TEMP B-TREE` for sorts.
flags: USE TEMP B-TREE FOR ORDER BY
toolkit.example:
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42 ORDER BY placed_at DESC;

toolkit.what: PostgreSQL: build an index without blocking writes. A plain CREATE INDEX blocks inserts and updates on the table until it finishes.
flags: no write lock; slower, and cannot run inside a transaction
toolkit.example: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY ix_orders_customer_placed ON orders (customer_id, placed_at DESC);

toolkit.what: Add non-key columns to an index so the query never touches the table: a covering index (PostgreSQL 11+, SQL Server). In SQLite, append the column to the index key instead.
flags: what you filter and sort on, equality columns first
extra columns carried only for reading
toolkit.example: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY ix_orders_customer ON orders (customer_id, placed_at) INCLUDE (total);

toolkit.what: Refresh the statistics the planner uses to estimate row counts (PostgreSQL and SQLite). After a big load or delete, stale statistics cause terrible plans.
flags: PostgreSQL normally does it for you, but can lag behind bulk changes

toolkit.what: PostgreSQL setting: log every statement slower than the threshold, with its duration. The cheapest way to catch slow queries you did not know about.
flags: an extension that also logs the plan of slow queries

steps.prompt: The customer page takes 800 ms. `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` shows this. What do you do?
code: Seq Scan on orders  (cost=0.00..116735.00 rows=12 width=64) (actual time=0.031..812.442 rows=12 loops=1)
options: Add an index on `orders (customer_id)`, built with `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`, then re-run the EXPLAIN to confirm an Index Scan
Run `ANALYZE orders`: the estimate is wrong
Increase the server's memory, since most pages were read from disk
steps.explain: It read 5 million rows to keep 12. The estimate (12) matches the actual (12), so statistics are fine: the plan has no better choice because there is no index. More memory would only make the full scan a little faster. (PostgreSQL 18 prints actual rows with decimals, `rows=12.00`, and on a table this size often splits the scan into a `Gather` over a `Parallel Seq Scan`; the reading is the same.)

steps.prompt: After last night's bulk import, a report that used to take 200 ms takes 40 seconds. The plan shows `Nested Loop (rows=1) (actual rows=480000)`. What is the most likely fix?
options: `ANALYZE` the imported tables, so the planner knows how many rows there are now
Rewrite the query as a CTE
steps.explain: The planner expected 1 row and got 480,000, so it chose a nested loop that is only good for tiny inputs. Fresh statistics after a bulk change usually bring the old plan back.

steps.prompt: Match each SQLite plan line to what it means.
pairs: reads every row of the table
looks up the rows through an index
answers from the index without reading the table
sorts the result in an extra step

steps.prompt: On a busy PostgreSQL table, add an index without blocking writes, and carry `total` so the query never visits the table.
steps.explain: `CONCURRENTLY` is PostgreSQL's non-blocking build (SQL Server's equivalent is `WITH (ONLINE = ON)`). `INCLUDE` adds a column that is stored but not part of the key.

steps.prompt: The dashboard got slow in production. Put the steps in order.
lines: Find the top queries by total_exec_time in pg_stat_statements
Run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on the worst one
Create the missing index with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY
Run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) again to confirm the new plan
Watch mean_exec_time drop for that query

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: Never guess at a slow query: find it by total time, read its real plan, change one thing and measure again. On a live PostgreSQL table every new index is `CONCURRENTLY`, and after any bulk load you run `ANALYZE`.
